FIXED the unbounded half, and CORRECTING a wrong claim I made when filing this.

WHAT SHIPPED

H.264 WebSocket streaming now runs on its own executor (streamPool, cached, daemon threads
named http-stream) instead of the 32-thread request pool. That was the unbounded case:
streamH264ToWebSocket sets setSoTimeout(0) and blocks for the whole viewing session, so on
the request pool each viewer PERMANENTLY removed a worker that the in-car UI's RPCs also
queue on. Ordinary requests are bounded by their 15 s socket timeout; a stream was bounded
by nothing.

A trap this nearly shipped with: handleClient ends in finally { client.close(); }. Handing
the socket to the stream pool and returning would have closed it immediately, killing every
live view the instant it started - while the pool-isolation tests still passed. Ownership is
now tracked explicitly (socketHandedOff), handleWebSocketUpgrade returns whether ownership
actually transferred, and a FAILED handshake deliberately returns false so that socket is
still closed rather than leaked. Both properties are pinned by tests.

VERIFIED ON THE HEAD UNIT after deploying:
  /ws upgrade still returns HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
  http-stream threads: 0 idle -> 1 while a stream is held open
So the handshake is intact, the socket survives the hand-off, and the stream is demonstrably
off the request pool.

CORRECTION - option 1 as I wrote it is NOT POSSIBLE

I said "the in-car UI is loopback and trivially identifiable - AuthMiddleware already
distinguishes it". That is wrong, and it is wrong for the same reason the security fix
earlier in this epic was needed: TOR CONNECTS TO 127.0.0.1:8080 TOO. Onion traffic is
indistinguishable from in-car traffic at the socket level - that is precisely why
AuthMiddleware had to stop trusting loopback and start checking whether a tunnel process is
running. It does not identify a connection's origin and cannot.

So reserving capacity "for loopback callers" would reserve it for remote clients as well.
Any real implementation needs a different discriminator - a header carrying the IPC token
(which never leaves the device, so a remote client cannot obtain it), or resolving the peer
port through /proc/net/tcp to the owning process. Both are more invasive than they sounded.

CORRECTION - keep-alive may not help this, and could hurt

BladeWatch-67h8 is still worth doing for LATENCY: ~1.4 s of Tor round trip per request is
paid because every response says Connection: close. But for POOL OCCUPANCY it is not
obviously a win and may be a loss: with a thread-per-connection model, keep-alive means
fewer connections each holding a worker for LONGER, across multiple requests. Do not land it
expecting it to fix starvation; measure occupancy before and after.

WHAT REMAINS

With streams moved off, the worst case on the request pool is now bounded: concurrent slow
Tor requests, each capped at the 15 s socket timeout. That is far better than unbounded, but
32 workers shared between the driver's screen and the public internet is still a coupling
worth removing. Reopen or file a follow-up if the in-car UI is still degraded under a real
remote load - and measure it with gfxinfo rather than by feel.

Catalogued 23 releases (alpha-v25.4 to alpha-v44.2, plus the braveheart/v48 channel tag) and the full source at commit 16468a3, into docs/evaluations/overdrive-release-catalogue.md. ~95 feature rows across the 8 domains plus an unassigned section, each with an introducing version, a DiLink hardware applicability flag and a source package. Two corrections to the brief are recorded in the document: the repo DOES publish complete source (848 java / 245 kt), and the release range starts at v25.4 not v33.1. Headline findings: 22 of 49 Overdrive packages have no BladeWatch counterpart, and the bulk of recent engineering is DiLink 5 camera work that cannot apply to a v3 head unit. 14 features exist only in source with no release note - notably the 38-file roadsense engine, an 8-file remote virtual-display control surface, ABRP telemetry, Telenav IPC, hotspot management and install analytics. Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-vehicle-adas.md. Every feature labelled cloud-only, local-SDK or either with evidence; DiLink v3 availability checked against BladeWatch source per feature rather than assumed; every actuating feature has a safety paragraph with an interlock proposal or a Skip; the ADAS diagnostics idea is assessed and recommended as the cheapest first step. Two findings dominate. First, Overdrive's own AdasBlindSpotProbe says the eight blind-spot ALERT registers have never been confirmed on a car and that the shipped code reads six fabricated ids - so the ADAS trigger features are an unfinished investigation, not a feature to port; the read-only probe and its adasFieldInventory dump are the thing worth taking, and BladeWatch cannot get the same data today because its ADAS reads log at DEBUG and R8 strips them in release. Second, and outside the task's list: BladeWatch has NO motion interlock anywhere - a repo-wide search finds no gear or speed check in VehicleCommandRouter, VehicleControlApiHandler or VehicleServiceImpl - while it already actuates windows, seats, climate and the tailgate motor. Overdrive's DrivingSafetyGuard is a pure, fail-closed, unit-testable gate and is recommended as a Port. Charge cap is already present and better instrumented here. Charging schedule and remote wake-up are cloud-only and Skipped. No vehicle command was sent and no device read was performed - CAR_IP was unset and adb listed no devices, so every v3 claim is labelled unverified rather than guessed.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-automations.md. BladeWatch has NO automation concept anywhere - no automation package, nothing in flutter_ui, web or proto - so every estimate is for building an engine: Overdrive's is 17,525 lines across 74 files plus 2,315 lines of HTTP handlers and 1,053 of community client. The trigger question is answered concretely with a signal-by-signal table: Overdrive registers 60 signals, BladeWatch already collects 102 telemetry fields, and about 45 of the 60 are observable today with no new telemetry work - the sensing layer is not the obstacle, the engine is. The 15 unavailable ones split into absent subsystems (mqtt, bluetooth, weather, telephony), unimplemented sensor reads (occupant, cpd, ambient, energyRegen) and three ADAS alert signals that the vehicle/ADAS evaluation showed rest on unconfirmed fabricated register ids. Engine placement: the DAEMON, not Flutter - actuation needs UID 2000, rules must outlive the Activity given ssc_skip and the missing BOOT_COMPLETED, and all 45 signals are already daemon-side; Flutter authors and displays only, over a new ConnectRPC service. Community sharing is a Skip: it needs a Cloudflare Worker plus D1 that BladeWatch does not have, the referenced community-edge backend directory is NOT present in the repo despite being called open-source, and adopting it means hosting user content, moderating reports and sending a persistent deviceId to a third party. Its no-shell plus import-as-disabled safety model is worth keeping if sharing is ever built. Key mapping is cheaper than expected because BladeWatch already ships KeepAliveAccessibilityService from the fork and can enable it via WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS - but its accessibility_service_config.xml declares zero event types, which Overdrive proved on a real DiLink unit means onKeyEvent is never dispatched; the fix is documented. Noted where I drew the toast/dialog line against the remote-communication task, and labelled the two large files I sized rather than read.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-ai-assistant.md. Per-answer-type data table covers all 14 of GenAiContext's context modes with the exact allowlisted fields each sends. The design is careful - field allowlists not blocklists, RoadSense hazards aggregated with coordinates withheld, a 12-rule log redactor - with ONE leak I flagged as unacceptable: recent_events sends place.short, a reverse-geocoded place name attached to surveillance events, which is a record of where the owner parks going to a third-party API, and the payload's own privacy string claims coordinates were omitted. BladeWatch would not hit it today only because it has no geo package. Key custody: do NOT port CredentialCipher - it AES-GCMs the key into the PUBLIC config.json with a device-id-derived key and a hardcoded salt, which is obfuscation not an access boundary, and it depends on byd/cloud/crypto which was deleted in 61b4d7f. Proposal is SecretConfigStore unchanged - mode 600 shell:shell, app writes once over the TCP command bridge and never reads back - which is strictly stronger and less work. Process: the DAEMON, and the reason is the key rather than convenience; a UI-side call would put a third-party credential in the app UID and discard the custody model. Noted that the call goes out over the car's own connection, not through Tor. Offline: retryOnConnectionFailure(false), no queue, no background attempts - correct for this device; on-demand is worth shipping degraded, scheduled insights are not, and scheduled generation is blocked anyway because Overdrive implements presets as ordinary time automations and BladeWatch has no engine. TFLite/YOLO assessed and called a red herring in three sentences rather than padded. Shippable subset stated: on-demand text only, five safe context modes, five of eleven rows Skipped.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-remote-communication.md. Domain splits cleanly: messages are cheap and the foundation exists, voice is expensive and carries the safety problem. AUDIO PATH: reported unverified as instructed - the head unit was unreachable. Architecturally, Overdrive does NOT play audio from the daemon; CabinAudioController is 42 lines that shell out to am start-foreground-service to run an app-UID service owning the AudioTrack, with audio framed daemon-to-app over a local socket. So the daemon's position outside the Activity lifecycle hurts here, uniquely. Noted BladeWatch's own precedent, AudioTestApiHandler, which pursued the AVAS exterior speaker via the BYD HAL rather than cabin audio, and that BladeWatch declares RECORD_AUDIO but not MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS. Proposed one non-destructive first check with dumpsys audio that settles feasibility before any of the 1290 lines are written. TRANSPORT: more nuanced than a flat Skip. 16 kHz PCM is 32 KB/s against 101 KB/s measured Tor throughput so bandwidth fits; push-to-talk is half-duplex so a 2s one-way delay is serviceable for an announcement even though it would ruin a conversation. The real risk is jitter - the jitter buffer is 113 lines, likely sized for LAN, and the 3s inactivity stop could cut a session on a stalled circuit. Messages over Tor are trivially fine. OVERLAY: StatusOverlayService IS a reusable basis - it already holds WindowManager, builds LayoutParams and degrades gracefully when SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW is missing, which is already declared. Recommended extending it rather than adding a second overlay owner, citing the translucent-bootstrap-window regression. SAFETY - the finding that should decide the domain: VehicleCommunicationSafety gates the voice OVERLAY on reverse/blind-spot/RoadSense but its own javadoc says audio continues underneath, and there is no gear or speed check on the audio path at all, so a remote party can make noise in a moving car. That compounds the already-recorded absence of any motion interlock in BladeWatch. emergencyDisabled is a config flag, not a rate limit. Recommendation: ship messages, skip voice until the audio path is proven and a real interlock exists; a LAN-only driving-gated variant would be a different feature. Line drawn with the automations task is stated identically in both documents.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-surveillance.md. The governing finding: almost nothing in this domain is a file to copy. Overdrive's versions of seven files BladeWatch already owns have grown 2x to 5.6x since the fork - GpuSurveillancePipeline 1772 to 9910, SurveillanceEngineGpu 3842 to 12785, ThumbnailBuffer 383 to 1085 - about 24,000 lines of divergence. Detection tuning and hero thumbnails are diffs inside shared code, not portable features, and any estimate treating them as ports is wrong by an order of magnitude. Overdrive also ships a 205-line DETECTION-INVARIANTS.md with four evidence channels, an S1-S7 funnel and six invariants; adopting that document costs nothing and is recommended independent of any code port. DETERRENT PANEL WAKE - addressed head-on and the answer is yes: state=ON with nothing visible is a backlight-off condition, not a sleeping display, and BYD exposes PowerManager.TurnBacklightOn(long) by reflection from UID 2000, which Overdrive uses as tier 1 and self-gates the WithLock escalation to DiLink 4 only. Crucially BladeWatch ALREADY HAS this primitive - AccSentryDaemon.java:1482 and :1490 with both casings, plus getPowerScreenStatus at :1110 and :1661 - used for the stealth panel, never for showing anything. So the deterrent's hardest prerequisite is solved and it is the one genuinely separable, genuinely new feature here; recommended Port with its driving guard, with two cautions drawn from the ADB-dialog limitation and the translucent-bootstrap focus regression. BATTERY - explicitly marked UNMEASURED, device unreachable; noted that BladeWatch has no idle FPS ramp at all and that AdaptiveBitrateController varies bitrate not frame rate so it does not touch the dominant per-frame cost, and that SocCutoffMonitor/BatteryVoltageMonitorV2 are more on point than idle FPS if drain is the real concern. Every feature checked against BladeWatch with a file reference; ten present-or-absent checks listed explicitly so nothing is recommended that already exists.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-camera-ux.md. Hardware filter stated once in a table with a per-item reason: the whole CHANGELOG camera block - QCarCam/AIS, fast_cam_capture, native 2x2 mosaic, abstract UNIX socket IPC, 4K HEVC ULTRA_4K, CarBodyManager.getShiftMode - is DiLink 5 and cannot apply, and the mosaic orientation fix is DiLink 4. Noted the one exception worth rescuing from that block: the parallel low-bitrate stream encoder architecture is generation-independent and relevant to Tor's 101 KB/s ceiling, though BladeWatch appears to have it already. PROJECTION was not the privilege Skip I expected. ClusterProjectionController documents, verified on-device, that uid 2000 shell is PLATFORM-SIGNED and so clears the OEM container service's checkSignatures gate - and BladeWatch's daemon runs as the same uid, so privilege is not the blocker. The real blockers are that projection is a FULL takeover which blanks the driver's instrument cluster for its duration, with gauge-restore on every exit path being the whole point of the class, and that v3 availability is unverified since it hardcodes CLUSTER_DISPLAY_ID=1 and a fission PresentationVirtualDisplay. Skipped on the gauge-blanking risk, not on privilege. ACC-AWARE SCALING is the substantive non-UX finding: GpuSurveillancePipeline and PanoramicCameraGpu contain no accOn/isAccOn/ACC_ON reference at all, so BladeWatch decides WHETHER to record by driving state but never varies how hard the pipeline works - the same class of problem as this cycle's responsiveness work, one layer down. UX ideas transfer but none of the 89 Android UI files do; recommended camera-first Live, and explicitly recommended AGAINST the collapsible rail because BladeWatch's nav_rail.dart is deliberately custom - Material's NavigationRailView caps collapsed items at 7 and BladeWatch has 9 destinations. Four recommendations plus three cheap verify-don't-build checks; everything else Skip.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-trips-energy.md. Established the BladeWatch baseline first, with evidence per capability. The order-of-magnitude question is answered: tariff cost accounting is a NEW SUBSYSTEM, not a small addition - Overdrive's charging package is 6,706 lines across 8 files, BladeWatch has no charging package, and tariffs sit atop a chain (trip cost needs a priced session needs a recorded session needs a calibrated energy counter) whose middle ~3,200 lines are entirely absent. CounterScaleCalibrator exists because the BMS energy counter's scale is untrustworthy, which is not a problem you discover from a spec. Proposed a genuinely small 80-percent alternative: extend TripConfig from one global rate to a short named list with an optional geofence reusing SafeLocationManager, pricing by trip start location - about a day's work. Charging detection DOES exist (ChargingDetector, session-level by design); the session ledger does not - GetLastCharge is backed by SoC history. KEY FINDING on the charging/gear interlock: half of it fixes a bug BladeWatch does not have. RecordingModeManager contains no gps/speed/isMoving/promote reference at all, so the GPS-drift gear promotion Overdrive had to inhibit cannot occur here - Overdrive added that fallback deliberately for unreliable DiLink 5 gear reads and then fixed the consequence. Parts 1 and 3 - force P while charging, suppress drive recording while charging - ARE applicable and absent, and are the best value-per-effort row in the domain since ChargingDetector already publishes session state. Kept the lesson: if BladeWatch ever adds a GPS movement fallback it must add the charging inhibit in the same change. VIN treated as the task required: Overdrive already defaults it OFF with an explicit auto-upload rationale; I set four conditions for porting (default off, warning at the point of enabling, never default-on for sentry clips) and flagged that TelemetryFields also declares LOCATION, the same PII class, which would be easy to wave through while scrutinising the VIN. PHEV rows marked owner-dependent rather than guessed. Six ordered recommendations plus three verify-don't-build checks.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-roadsense-nav.md. WHAT ROADSENSE IS, in two sentences: it turns the head unit's IMU into a road-surface sensor - driving over a speed bump or pothole produces an accel/gyro signature that is classified, severity-scored, GPS-tagged and written to a local spatial store; those hazards are shared with other drivers via a Cloudflare edge service and chime plus overlay when you approach a known one. Established BladeWatch's baseline first: it ALREADY has map rendering on both clients (flutter_map 8.3.2 on MAPNIK in-car, Leaflet on web), GPS and geofencing - what it lacks is routing, guidance, geocoding, hazard detection and offline tiles. NETWORK: four third-party services enumerated with endpoints, keys and licence position - OpenFreeMap vector tiles (no key, ODbL attribution due), roadsense-edge Cloudflare Worker (source NOT in repo), Stadia Maps Valhalla routing (API key), ABRP/Iternio - plus Nominatim, Overpass and open-meteo. Flagged that THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md mentions NONE of MapLibre, OpenFreeMap, OSM/ODbL, Valhalla or Stadia, so porting the map stack inherits an under-documented licence position. AT 100 KM/H: answered with the formula - d = max(v*warnLeadSeconds, warnFloorMeters), defaults 4.0s and 30m, so about 111m or four seconds of lead, one ToneGenerator chime per hazard per approach, heading-gated at 2.5 m/s, with priority over Voice of God. Assessed that BladeWatch ships nothing comparable and that adding a safety-adjacent noise at a moving driver is a product decision with a liability shape, not a feature port. PRIVACY: per-feature table of exactly what leaves the device, with the standout being ABRP sending exact lat/lon, heading, elevation, odometer, speed and SoC continuously while driving to api.iternio.com, and hazard sharing pairing exact coordinates with a stable device id. Four-point minimum proposal including coarsening to a geohash cell, noting Overdrive already applies that discipline inside its AI context builder but not on the sync path. VERDICT: Skip the domain - not on hardware grounds, which is unusual in this epic, but because it is a second product bolted onto a dashcam. Three small rows survive: VehicleMotionEstimator for marker smoothing, Telenav IPC as the cheap way to reach the car's own nav, and saved places as an extension of SafeLocationManager. Also recorded that RoadSenseController's class doc is STALE - it claims nothing references it yet, but CameraDaemon and SurveillanceIpcServer both do and IMU_BATCH is wired; I nearly reported it as dead code on that comment's strength.

Wrote docs/evaluations/overdrive-integration-shortlist.md. Single ranked Port/Adapt table of 17 rows sorted by value per effort, deliberately not padded - ten further defensible items were judged below the line and left in their domain documents rather than promoted, and three verify-don't-build checks sit outside the table. Two large all-or-nothing items (the automation engine and the AI assistant) are held apart from the ranking because neither is worth a fraction of itself. Blocked section groups everything ruled out by reason - BYD Cloud gone, DiLink 4/5 only, needs an absent backend, needs a removed daemon, unsafe, already implemented - one line each, so these are not re-proposed in six months. Overlaps reconciled into single rows and noted: toast/dialog across automations and remote-communication, the AC switch-off timer across vehicle-adas and trips-energy, AI-authored automations blocked on the engine. Top 5 with a paragraph each, every one carrying its dependency and a concrete first step: the motion interlock, the ADAS diagnostic probe, adopting DETECTION-INVARIANTS.md, charging recording suppression, and the Screen Deterrent. Eight open questions for the developer. MIT attribution obligation recorded as applying to every Port/Adapt row. Flagged four weaknesses in the material including my own: nothing was verified on the car in any of the eight evaluations so this is a source study not a feasibility study; the L on detection tuning is not a number and rests on an unresolved question about whether BladeWatch's engine is an earlier version of Overdrive's or independently diverged, which changes the effort several-fold; the 45-of-60 available signals figure is an upper bound from source that should be re-measured before it justifies the engine decision; and three L estimates are size-based guesses. Also recorded that RoadSenseController's stale class doc nearly led me to report the largest package in the epic as dead code, with the lesson to trust call sites over headers. Document closes by stating explicitly that NO implementation issues were filed and that the next agent must not open them until the developer picks.

All ten children closed. Produced docs/evaluations/ containing the shared release catalogue, eight domain evaluations and a ranked integration shortlist. Outcome: 17 Port/Adapt rows, a Blocked section grouped by reason so ruled-out features are not re-proposed, a Top 5 with concrete first steps, and eight open questions for the developer. No implementation issues filed by design - the developer picks from the shortlist first, then issues get written against that decision.

Done and verified. The last open criterion said the workflow had not yet been exercised on GitHub and needed four signing secrets plus a tag push. Both parts have since resolved. The design changed: both APKs now build UNSIGNED and the workflow needs no secrets at all, failing the build if either APK IS signed or if fewer than two are produced - signing happens afterwards with apksigner using one key for both, which is what the shared UID requires. And it has been exercised: gh run list shows one run, conclusion success, event push, tag v1.3.0.0, 13m21s. Triggers are tags v* plus workflow_dispatch only, so ordinary pushes and PRs build nothing. This session also added the missing half of the original intent - tags: v* fires for a tag on ANY branch, so a feature-branch tag could publish an official-looking release from unmerged code. A Refuse to release a tag that is not on main step now runs git merge-base --is-ancestor against origin/main, exempting workflow_dispatch so an existing release can be deliberately re-run. Both paths were dry-run: v1.3.0.0 resolves as on main and exits 0, a synthetic orphan commit exits 1 and fails the build. A bug introduced in that step's first draft - git fetch origin main --depth=0, which is invalid and would have failed the next release - was caught and replaced with an explicit refspec. actionlint passes the new step clean.

Wrote docs/evaluations/electro-feature-catalogue.md. Bundle index-WOOEUslN.js (4,032,903 bytes) - the SAME hash the issue recorded on 2026-09-14, so no deploy in between and this describes that build. Brace-matched the i18next resources object out of the bundle and parsed 1,940 English key/value pairs; 16 languages ship, not the eight expected (pt en el es it fr ru tr he de vi ar ja th pl ko). /changelog is NOT readable without signing in - HTTP 200 but the body is byte-identical to the 1,760-byte landing shell, a client-rendered SPA route - and I did not sign in. Did NOT write electro-ui-strings.md: 1,940 strings of someone else's product copy in a public repo is republishing, and every string a sibling needs is quoted as evidence in the catalogue. PT-only keys number 12 and are not a hidden feature - all twelve are APK install steps for Modern 2507 Plus firmware. Three structural findings reframe the epic. First, Electro is a paid cloud SaaS - US.99/month billed annually at US.88 per car, multi-device and multi-user, with trials and coupons - so its account, subscription and relay model is not portable at all. Second, the automation builder IS the product: 584 of 1,940 keys, 30 percent of the entire UI surface, and I extracted the full 59 triggers, 77 actions and 46 variables verbatim so no sibling re-mines the bundle. Third, THERE IS NO STANDALONE ADAS PAGE - every ADAS and driving-mode control is an automation action, so ntum.3 is mis-scoped and overlaps ntum.5 almost entirely; the catalogue says so and asks those two to agree a line. Also flagged that this is a source-free evaluation, unlike the Overdrive epic, so no effort estimate derived from it can be trusted the same way. Unassigned section leads with 'Avoid reboot routine' - BYD firmware runs a scheduled reboot that disconnects the app, suppressible on 2508+ until the next manual reboot - which is an operational fact about hardware BladeWatch also fights for daemon uptime.

Wrote docs/evaluations/electro-vehicle-comfort.md. The task warned this domain has the highest chance of recommending something that already exists, and that proved right: of 17 comfort controls Electro exposes, BladeWatch already has 9. Critically, the task nominated window and sunroof percentage control as the good test case for whether the local SDK exposes a position or only open/close - it exposes a position and BladeWatch ALREADY USES IT. MoveWindowRequest carries optional int32 target_percent with explicit-presence semantics, and the proto comment explains why the optional is load-bearing: 0 percent is a default scalar that would be omitted from JSON and silently route a close-fully request down the direction path instead of the closed-loop positioning path. That is a detail you only write after the feature works. Indexes 5 and 6 cover sunroof and sunshade on the same message, so the roof-curtain row is Present too. Second direct question - what BladeWatch does when the car powers down - also comes back Present: DaemonKeepaliveService holds a PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK and the daemons are ACC-aware. Drain cost explicitly marked UNMEASURED rather than estimated, since the device was unreachable and the meaningful measurement is 12V draw over hours, not CPU percent - a distinction this project has already paid for. Noted that parked cost today is dominated by surveillance, which has no idle FPS ramp, and that Overdrive SocCutoffMonitor and BatteryVoltageMonitorV2 are more on point than anything in this domain if drain is the real concern. Recommended four small cabin-only rows: AC auto/fan-only (backed by Overdrive fixing AC Auto specifically on DiLink 3.0, the strongest v3 signal in either epic), defrosters, media volume/mute, and screen on/off where AccSentryDaemon already has the turnBacklightOn primitive. Skipped instrument-cluster projection on the gauge-blanking argument, reinforced by Electro own UI warning that an ADAS rectangle is drawn and cannot be removed. Flagged that every Adapt row lands in BladeWatch ungated actuation path, so the DrivingSafetyGuard interlock should precede all of them. Also cautioned that Electro supports many BYD models, so a string proves a feature on SOME car, not on a v3.

Wrote docs/evaluations/electro-adas-modes.md. Started with the safety question as the task directs. The decisive structural fact: Electro exposes all 18 driving controls as AUTOMATION ACTIONS, so they can fire unattended from a rule written weeks earlier with no human in the loop at the moment of actuation. Grouped every control by worst realistic outcome. Group 1, crash-avoidance (AEB, emergency lane keeping, lane assist, forward collision warning, cross-traffic BRAKING): recommendation is SKIP the disable direction, and I declined to propose an interlock rather than inventing a plausible one - the interlock that would make disabling a crash system acceptable is human confirmation at the moment of actuation, and automation removes precisely that; a parked-only plus confirm-on-save gate would look like an answer and would not be one, because the rule fires later when nobody is asked. The task said Skip is a perfectly good result here and that is the result. Noted Overdrive independently reached the same place - its v33.0 notes say Emergency Braking is re-arm-only, never off. Group 2 warnings: Adapt, low priority, only with visible state. Group 3 handling modes (steering, braking, suspension, drive mode, regen, iTAC): Adapt but ONLY after a motion interlock exists, since the hazard is a change in the control loop the driver is inside, mid-corner. Group 4 reporting: no interlock needed. Reading versus writing answered: reads are safe and cheap, writes carry every risk, and BladeWatch write surface today is SetAdas exposing speed-limit-warning ONLY despite 29 declared ADAS ids - and per the Overdrive epic a declared id proves nothing because resolveOrFallback silently substitutes a literal, so availability is honestly unknown for every write row. One read-only probe settles the whole column. Also recorded a scoping correction: there is no standalone ADAS surface in Electro, so this task overlaps ntum.5 almost entirely; I drew the line explicitly - this document owns safety and per-control availability, ntum.5 owns the engine, and ntum.5 should not re-litigate these. Found one thing Electro tells us that Overdrive did not: Electro own UI says an ADAS rectangle is drawn on the projected cluster and cannot be removed, independently corroborating the Skip on cluster projection.

Wrote docs/evaluations/electro-cameras.md. Of 28 camera features Electro exposes, 14 are already present in BladeWatch, each listed with a file reference rather than assumed. The brief specifically asked me to verify safe locations before proposing them - they exist (SafeLocationManager, SafeLocation, a SafeLocations ConnectRPC service and a web page section), as does time-window scheduling (SurveillanceSchedule with overnight spans). Also recorded one thing BladeWatch has that Electro does not: proximity recording off all 8 BYD parking radar sensors, with nothing corresponding in Electro 1,940 strings. The most important row is the still-frame fallback the brief spotted from the refreshing-frame state. It matters more for BladeWatch than for Electro because of this project own measured onion numbers - 101 KB/s sustained, TTFB 1.4 to 2.2s warm - and because live view reaches Tor Browser only via the MSE plus jmuxer fallback, since Tor Browser has no WebCodecs decoder; a periodic JPEG needs no decoder at all. I handled the awkward part explicitly: BladeWatch-gpik, which I closed earlier in this same session, DELETED the /snapshot route. That was right on its evidence - the route could never return a frame and its own rule said remove unless the live-view work went the snapshot route, which it did not. This proposal does not reverse it and says so: what was deleted was a route advertising a capability nothing implemented; what is proposed is a degradation path for slow links, retaining an already-encoded frame, which is the shape the original issue itself anticipated. If built it needs the frame-size measurement gpik asked for and never got. Other genuinely new rows: OEM DVR app toggle, recording priority Performance vs Reliability, and the storage-budget deletion-confirmation dialog that warns before lowering a limit destroys clips. Deliberately marked the sentry deterrent message and the side camera as CORROBORATION rather than new rows, because both already have homes in the Overdrive shortlist and listing them here would double-count. Two corroborations recorded: Electro own UI states cabin audio is unavailable with ACC off, which strengthens the Skip on Voice of God, and both competitors integrate with the car OEM DVR while BladeWatch has no integration at all.

Wrote docs/evaluations/electro-automations.md. Answered all four brief questions. (1) BladeWatch has NO automation concept - established by repo-wide search in the Overdrive epic; the two closest things, SurveillanceSchedule and SafeLocationManager, are hardcoded single-purpose and daemon-side, and are arguably the first two rules an engine would subsume. (2) Produced an actual trigger list: of Electro 59 triggers, about 38 are ALREADY POLLED by BladeWatch (speed, SoC, 12V, cabin and outside temp, charging start/end, car on/off, selector, doors, drive mode, turn signal, headlights, seat belts, internet, schedule, geofence, sentry motion) and about 21 would need new work, of which eleven are the steering-wheel button events. - HttpResponse.connectionHeader(out): the single place the Connection header is now decided. All 17 previously hardcoded sites across 4 files route through it, and it degrades to close for any unwrapped stream, so a writer reached by a future path keeps the old always-correct behaviour.

Loopback never saw it because /status goes through the main dispatch chain, which loops correctly, and /login.html does not. Over Tor, request 2 got an empty status line. Those three now stay on the connection. Both auth-rejection gates now set keepAlive=false before checkAuth writes its 401 and restore it afterwards, so a rejection announces close honestly.

Only connection and rendezvous setup is amortisable, and that is the 0.58s. Acceptance criterion 2 as literally worded (TTFB materially below 1.4s) is therefore unreachable and was accepted as written-on-a-wrong-premise rather than met. Fixed and verified on the head unit.

CAUSE. Content-Length counts BYTES; the body was read with BufferedReader.read(char[]), which returns CHARACTERS. Under a UTF-8 decoder those differ for any non-ASCII body, so the read loop asked for more chars than could ever arrive and blocked until the socket timeout.

FIX. The request reader now decodes as ISO-8859-1, which maps bytes 0-255 bijectively onto chars 0-255, so one char IS one byte and Content-Length is satisfied exactly. A new package-private HttpServer.decodeRequestBody(char[], int) narrows those chars back to bytes and decodes them as UTF-8. Checked that nothing else depends on the reader decoding UTF-8: every header the parser looks at (connection, content-length, sec-websocket-key, upgrade, range, if-none-match, cookie, authorization, content-type, connect-protocol-version, x-vehicle-action-token, accept-language, host, x-forwarded-*) is ASCII by nature, and a non-ASCII path arrives percent-encoded.

TESTS. New RequestBodyDecodingTest covers ASCII, empty, accented Latin, Japanese, Russian, Thai, Arabic, a 4-byte emoji, respecting the length argument over a slack buffer, and byte-value preservation. Each asserts the char count equals the UTF-8 byte count, which is the property that was violated. Mutation-tested: reverting decodeRequestBody to the old new String(chars, 0, length) fails four of them while the ASCII cases still pass - exactly the shape of the bug.

VERIFIED ON DEVICE, POSTing real bodies over the forwarded loopback:
  ASCII                   0.19s  200
  accented, 2 bytes/char  0.09s  200
  Japanese, 3 bytes/char  0.05s  200
  emoji, 4 bytes/char     0.04s  200
All prompt; before the fix the three non-ASCII cases would have blocked for the full 15s socket timeout.

REGRESSION CHECKS after the charset change, since it touches how every request line and header is read: keep-alive reuse still works (connects=1 then 0,0,0) and the WebSocket upgrade still returns 101 with Sec-WebSocket-Accept HSmrc0sMlYUkAGmm5OPpG2HaGWk=, which is the known-correct hash for the key sent - so Sec-WebSocket-Key survived the Latin-1 read intact.

Done, test-first, in Kotlin. Wrote FisheyeDewarpMappingTest.kt before the implementation, then added mapDetectionsToSource to FisheyeDewarp.kt to pass it.

WHAT IT DOES. Maps YOLO's boxes from dewarped crop space back to the original warped space using the same forward sampling transform the pixels used, evaluated at the four corners PLUS the four edge midpoints, taking the bounding box of the mapped set. Eight points rather than four because the transform is radial: a straight edge bows, so a box's extreme can sit at an edge midpoint, and a corners-only mapping clips the subject out of its own box. Order and size are preserved because downstream code indexes the list positionally. Fails open by returning the ORIGINAL list, never null and never a dropped entry.

TYPE CHECK THE TASK ASKED FOR. Confirmed against the data class rather than assumed: BladeWatch's Detection is Kotlin, constructed as (classId, confidence, x, y, w, h), which happens to match Overdrive's Java constructor order. Being Kotlin-to-Kotlin now, properties are accessed directly (d.x, d.classId) rather than through generated getters.

SEVEN TESTS, each pinning something a plausible mistake would break: identity on a non-dewarped quadrant, null and empty handled, classId/confidence/order preserved, a centred box staying put, bounds and non-negative extents at all four edges and both slivers, the 8-point versus 4-corner height comparison, and a ROUND TRIP.

The round trip is the one that matters most and it is not in the original: paint a marker at a known source position, dewarp the image, locate the marker in dewarped space, feed that back as a detection, and require it to map home within a few pixels. Every other test checks a function against the formula; this one checks the two halves of the feature against EACH OTHER. A consistent sign error in both would pass everything else and still put boxes in the wrong place.

MUTATION TESTED, three ways, each caught by the test written for it: dropping the edge midpoints fails the 8-point test; replacing classId and confidence with constants fails the preservation test; and inverting the transform in the mapping alone - dividing where it should multiply, so the mapping no longer matches the pixels - fails the round trip.

     camera            events   blind   rate
     left   (mirror)       84      68    81%
     right  (mirror)       11      10    91%
     front                  8       0     0%
     rear                   1       0     0%

   mirror combined 78/95 = 82% blind, front+rear 0/9 = 0%, Fisher exact two-sided p = 1.1e-06.

   A motion event seen only by a mirror camera classifies nothing about 82% of the time. That is the signature this feature targets and it independently supports the quadrant choice: dewarp Q1 and Q3, leave Q0 and Q2 at zero.

2. The transform does what it should, visually. EVIDENCE IT TARGETS A REAL PROBLEM HERE. Measured on this car across 196 events: a motion event seen only by a mirror camera classifies nothing 82% of the time, against 0% for front and rear (p = 1.1e-06).

WHAT IS NOT PROVEN. The constants are still Overdrive's, unverified on this vehicle - BladeWatch-3dg8 was closed with its after-measurement waived by the developer. So the feature is known to be safe and known to target a real symptom, but is NOT yet known to improve detection here. The class doc and that issue both say so.

Fail-open by construction: any error returns the original crop and unmapped boxes, front and rear are at strength 0 which is byte-identical to no dewarp, and setting all strengths to 0 disables it entirely with the wiring guard still passing.
